newsitem.title: UK: Adams says Britain's Blair could boost peace.
newsitem.headline: Adams says Britain's Blair could boost peace.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, said new British Prime Minster Tony Blair had the power to revitalise Northern Ireland's quest for peace on Sunday and pledged he too would play his part.
But Adams, speaking after U.S. President Bill Clinton called for an Irish Republican Army truce, signalled that the conditions demanded by the IRA were not yet in place.
The British province has been more unstable in recent months after a series of IRA attacks here and in England which prompted revenge strikes by pro-British Protestant guerrillas.
Adams's election to parliament along with another senior Sinn Fein party official last Friday was seen by Irish media as strengthening peace hopes.

But Adams told Irish radio that Sinn Fein must have a seat in all-party negotiations to help rebuild the shattered peace process. Britain says the IRA must first call a ceasefire, a demand the guerrillas have repeatedly spurned.
"I think what we need to do is first of all to get all of the vexed and contentious issues which have blocked...the search for peace so far," the Sinn Fein leader said.
"In other words, we need a credible, real talks process. The IRA has made its position quite clear that it will enhance...such a peace process."
After British Labour's sweeping victory, President Clinton, who supports joint British and Irish peace efforts, urged a new momentum to end the province's years of strife.

"I hope and pray now that the British election is over that Prime Minister Blair will take up the torch, that the IRA will declare a ceasefire and that we can get back on the road to resolving that problem," he told reporters in the U.S.
Sinn Fein supporters held a march in West Belfast on Sunday to commemorate IRA hunger-strikers who died in prison in 1981 and celebrate Sinn Fein's Friday election victories.
In County Londonderry, extra police were drafted in to re-route a controversial parade by Protestants through the mainly Catholic nationalist village of Bellaghy.
Adams in his radio interview urged Blair, who swept John Major's minority Conservatives from office in a landslide victory, to implement key reforms in Northern Ireland.

"I think the biggest issue out of the election is the fact that this Labour administration has such a magnificient majority. If there is the political will, therefore, Mr Blair will be able to move forward in a way that could be quite unprecedented."

Irish nationalists criticised Major, accusing him of stalling progress towards full peace by horse-trading for parliamentary support with the province's majority Protestant pro-British to stay in power in his final months.

Mo Mowlam, the woman appointed by Blair as his chief Northern Ireland minister, challenged Sinn Fein on Saturday to persuade the IRA to forsake violence so as to win Sinn Fein a talks place. "The ball is in Sinn Fein's court."
